claims: Since 1 July 2022, all employees, including casuals, are entitled to SG regardless of how much they earn
whys: Removing the $450 threshold did not remove the under-18 rule: employees under 18 who work 30 hours or less a week are still not entitled to SG, and the same 30-hour rule applies to private or domestic workers. As written, 'all employees' overstates who is covered.
constants: SUPER_GUARANTEE (lib/constants) could hold the under-18 / 30-hour eligibility rule

claims: A common benchmark is 1x your annual salary by age 30
carry-forward ... total super balance is under ${formatAUD(500_000)}
carry-forward ... when your total super balance is under $500,000
whys: The benchmark is unsourced and unattributed. The page's AUDIT does not allow editorial judgment, so it reads as a rule.
The $500,000 carry-forward threshold is typed as a literal in the FAQ rather than read from a constant.
The rule omits the timing condition: the total super balance test is measured at 30 June of the previous financial year. Unused cap amounts also expire after 5 years.
constants: n/a (needs a source, or a labelled editorial view)

claims: Two strategies legally reduce your taxable income and increase your after-tax pay: salary sacrifice and work-related deductions.
Two strategies ... increase your after-tax pay: salary sacrifice and work-related deductions
whys: Salary sacrifice lowers the amount paid to your bank account. The page's own strategy table (line 346) says 'Increases Bank Deposit? No (funds go to super)'. It saves tax overall but does not increase after-tax pay. The section also has a third strategy (private health insurance), but that one does not reduce taxable income, so the count of two is defensible.
Salary sacrifice lowers your bank deposit (the page's own table at line 346 says so). It saves tax overall but does not increase after-tax pay.
